Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. After prior consultations, I understand that the House is disposed to give its unanimous consent so that the parliamentary task force on Pension Reform may table its report at this time.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PRESENTATION OF FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: We agree.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PRESENTATION OF FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The House has heard the proposal of the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith). Is it agreed?

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: PRESENTATION OF FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the first report of the parliamentary task force on Pension Reform in both official languages to which, pursuant to Standing Order 69(13), the committee requests a comprehensive response.
[Editor's note: For above report, see today's Votes and Proceedings.]

The House resumed, from Tuesday, December 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-2, an Act to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to make related amendments to the Canada Pension Plan and the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I should inform the House that when debate adjourned at the previous sitting on Bill C-2, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans) had the floor. He had completed his 20-minute speech. The period is now open to questions and comments, if Hon. Members so wish. Otherwise, we will proceed to debate.

Mr. Speaker, I was wondering if the Parliamentary Secretary was of the same opinion as I am that there are no members of this House who can really say they thoroughly understand the Income Tax Act and, indeed, this Bill now before the House.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, is the Parliamentary Secretary saying to this House that he, as a Parliamentary Secretary, has no problem with this Bill, that he thoroughly understands all the clauses contained in it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we went through this Bill in the Finance Committee. We went into great detail when asking about the provisions. We received information as to the implications of those provisions. With regard to whether individual members had the complete knowledge of the technical details of the legislation, I would say probably not. However, members have been fully apprised of the implications of each of the provisions that was of concern to members of the committee. That is our role. We are not meant to be technical tax practitioners. We are to understand what the implications are of the legislation for actual practice by our constituents, the people of Canada. That is our job, not to be technical tax practitioners.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and other members of the committee went into great depth in many areas with regard to the Ways and Means motions. I think there is sufficient understanding by those members and, through them, other Members of the House to make a very rational judgment on this legislation. Quite frankly, that rational judgment would be passed very quickly because, as I said before, only two submissions were received by the committee that were relevant to the legislation, even though we had advertised nationally for submissions from every Canadian.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary has served with some considerable distinction as the Chairman of the Finance Committee. During his term as Chairman, two different Ministers of Finance asked the Committee to consider Ways and Means motions and to report back. Would the Parliamentary Secretary like to take a couple of moments to reflect on the process that his Committee went through and give us his reactions as to the value of that process for the future?

December 15, 1983
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be very happy to do that. It was a very enjoyable experience that I had as Chairman of that Committee. It was with regret that I stepped down as Chairman as a result of assuming new responsibilities. I would say that that was an excellent procedure which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) established of sending Ways and Means motions to the Finance Committee. He asked us to advertise nationally for submissions and to have those submissions and witnesses appear before us in order to make the views and concerns of Canadians known with regard to the tax legislation, and then to put forward recommendations for change. We did that earlier on in the year with regard to the first Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance and the Ways and Means motions that had been presented to us led to a number of changes in the legislation.
The April Budget was then brought down, the Ways and Means motions were put to us in the summer and the Finance Committee undertook the same process and again reported, with very little recommendation for change in this case because the public reaction to the Ways and Means motions and the April Budget had been so good that there was no need for us to make major changes.
That is the Bill that is before us now. I think it is a good Bill and I think the process it has gone through is an excellent one.
I think that process should be continued, and in light of the good work that the Committee did when examining this legislation, I think we should move expeditiously to pass the legislation.

Mr. Speaker, would the Parliamentary Secretary not agree that he is misleading the House in the sense that the Committee only dealt with a very small part of the legislation? The legislation before us deals, for example, with the indexed security plan which, from my calculations to date after having gone very carefully through the Bill, now covers some 20 clauses of the Bill. I was wondering if, in that respect, the Parliamentary Secretary could justify the inclusion of puts and calls as the kinds of securities that should be held behind indexed securities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to agree with the Hon. Member that the ISIPs and certain aspects of investment tax credits were not part of the Ways and Means motions that were referred to us. However, I should add that they were widely disseminated in the community at large and widely commented upon. The inclusion of the puts and calls as a possible investment within an ISIP was in response to a request made by the investment dealers themselves to try to broaden the scope.
If the Hon. Member is asking if we should find a way of indexing the value of all types of assets to inflation and only taxing the real appreciation of all types of assets instead of just the ones that happen to fit into an ISIP. I would say yes, I agree. That is what we have to move toward, but the ISIP is a first step which has never been taken before in Canada. It is a
first step toward realizing that only the after-inflation increase in value should be taxed. I believe that it is an excellent first step and I commend the Minister for taking that forward-looking first step. However, I would agree with the Hon. Member that we should not stop there but should go on to find ways of ensuring that taxation applies only to the real increase in the value of assets as opposed to the total inflationary increase in assets.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) has long been concerned about ISIPs. In fact, he has taken considerable time to oppose them in the House. He feels that they favour the big guy and hurt the small guy. I would like to make a further comment on that matter and point out to the Hon. Member that the cure recommended by the Tories for this problem would in fact hurt the small guy even more.
The removal of capital gains tax could in fact help the big guy at the expense of the small taxpayer who has no capital gains but only employment income. The distortion of our tax system by the removal of the capital gains tax would in fact go further than the Hon. Member claims. It would hurt the small business sector and would hurt the small taxpayer much more than the big taxpayer. I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to comment on this and perhaps give us his views on the matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker I think I would have to condition my response. Given the existing tax structure, there is no doubt that we must have a capital gains tax. Under the existing structure, the non-taxation of capital gains presented a major problem which was addressed by the Carter Commission and led to the introduction of the capital gains tax. I have proposed a way of solving that problem so that there would be no need for a capital gains tax. I contend that the fundamental problems which lead to the capital gains tax can be solved, and through my proposal there would be no leakage and therefore it would not be needed. Given the existing structure, however, a capital gains tax is essential in order to stop the leakages. I suggest that if the basic structure were fixed there would be no need for a capital gains tax.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Parliamentary Secretary for his explanation of the way he sees changes that could simplify the Income Tax Act. To some extent I agree with many of his proposals. For example, his proposal to merge dividends with all distributions and to have one tax system that integrated corporate and personal tax makes a great deal of sense. That would certainly remove the need for a capital gains tax and would simplify the Act.
I wonder if the Parliamentary Secretary had put his mind to the concept of Part VII tax and Part VIII tax which was not dealt with by the Committee. I refer to the investment tax credits and passing those back through to proposed purchasers of shares, the research tax credit in Part VIII where the company has to pay the money in as a tax and then apply for a
December 15, 1983

refund. This simplification process is now so complicated that I suggest he cannot understand it. I have a hard time understanding it and I am sure even the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fisher) cannot understand it. I wonder if the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans) could explain how the simplification of the Income Tax Act would be promoted by this step?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Perhaps by unanimous consent the Parliamentary Secretary might be allowed to give a brief answer.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated, the existing structure of the tax system requires the kind of measures the Government wanted to take to allow more equity capital to be raised by companies in order to provide more funding for research and development, and that is basically the only way that result could be achieved. Unless we are prepared to change the structure of the tax system to a more simplified but equally effective structure from the point of view of raising revenue, the kinds of measures we need in order to stimulate research and development, to stimulate investment and to stimulate the provision of equity capital for small businesses are going to be complex.
That is why I think, and the Minister agrees, as does the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, that we must move forward with the simplification process. That is why the Minister referred that subject matter to the Standing Committee, in order to find a way to simplify it, beginning with the small business tax system. I would say that the whole structure needs to be thought out again, perhaps not in radical ways but certainly in fundamental ways.

Mr. Speaker, the customary remark made by the most Members when they rise to deal with legislation by way of debate is that it is a pleasure for them to have an opportunity to participate. It is certainly not a pleasure for me on this occasion. We are confronted with a monstrous piece of legislation in terms of complexity and length, and that is Bill C-2, to amend the Income Tax Act.
A number of recent occurrences have a substantial bearing on our deliberations today. Yesterday in the House the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres), who is responsible for the administration of this Act which is sought to be amended, had occasion to comment upon a number of questions directed to him with respect to the way in which his officials have carried out their duties. He used with regularity the phrase "It is the duty of my officials to see that taxpayers pay their fair share of tax". He also with some regularity referred to the word "equity". In the event, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister has any knowledge of the way in which his Department functions, he will recognize that there is about as much fairness in the functioning of that Department as there is in an armed robbery. He will also recognize that the courts themselves have said that there is no equity in tax law.
Income Tax Act
What we are confronted with is a statute of precise nature which will be interpreted without any regard to equity by the tax courts of this country. It is, therefore, abundantly clear to anyone who knows that very simple fact that it is incumbent upon Hon. Members of this House to be particularly careful with a statute which has built within it the right granted to a department of government to move against the property and assets of a citizen, seize them, take them away and sell them, which is indeed what this Act permits.
Accordingly, I am dismayed to find that we should have members of the Government recommending that we speedily attend to the passage of this legislation. Some reference was made a few moments ago by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans) with respect to a simplification process which was begun, according to him, by a simple reference to a committee of the House for examination and study by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). The fact of the matter is that it has been recognized for some long time that this Act has got completely out of hand. It goes beyond the comprehension and understanding not only of the average citizen, against whom its provisions apply, but some of the most competent and able tax practitioners in the country.
Our process here today is one of adding to the complexity in a fashion which does nothing to remove the fundamental problem of undue complication, an undue complication which must be faced by the citizens of the nation when they endeavour to comply with the law which this House passes. Not long ago, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce had an opportunity to make a submission to the Minister of Finance, and in the very introduction of its presentation made the following remarks:
We are pleased that a serious study is now being made of ways to simplify the Income Tax Act. We recognize that the Act must be complex in certain provisions, but the provisions now in place relating to the taxation of small corporate businesses are overwhelming in their complexity. Furthermore, the introduction of the corporate distributions tax, especially in its anti-avoidance provisions, will introduce uncertainties and complexities into the Act totally out of proportion to any useful result. For example, the anti-avoidance provision dealing with amalgamations and liquidations has the effect (unintended we hope) of imposing a penalty tax on normal purchase transactions which will arise in the future, in circumstances where it can be easily demonstrated that no advantage has been gained by the taxpayer.
The introduction to the submission concludes with the following remark:
We are also concerned that the growth of complexity will further fuel the development of the so-called "underground economy", a development which we regard as unhealthy.
And indeed, Mr. Speaker, any citizen who is aware of what is happening, that his property can be taken from him by the Government, will be alarmed when he examines the tabulation of statistics prepared by the Department of National Revenue in 1982. A few dollars short of $42 billion were taken out of the pockets of individual Canadian citizens. That is up from $33.88 billion the year before.

December 15, 1983
Income Tax Act
This is the most serious issue facing this Elouse, Mr. Speaker. How long can it continue that 50 per cent of the total GNP of this nation is being spent by government? With this Government's share of that expenditure increasing at an alarming rate, is it not appropriate that we begin examining a process not only to simplify the provisions of this Act, which this Bill does not do, but to give back to the people who work in Canada to produce the wealth more of what they have indeed produced? That is the only way for genuine recovery.
If we examine the recent Speech from the Throne we find some rather interesting comments. We are told that:
Small scale entrepreneurs are the unsung heroes of the recovery.
According to the Speech from the Throne. It goes on to say:
Small businesses are a perpetual source of inventiveness, valuable export earnings, and vast job creation potential.
How, indeed, is a small-scale entrepreneur, the unsung hero of the recovery and the creator of vast job potential, treated in this Act, in particular in the Bill before the House? Well, he is left to languish and suffer while others take advantage of the Indexed Security Investment plan which takes up a large measure of the provisions of this Bill. Touted as an opportunity and a first step by government to index the real growth of capital gains in our country so that the tax impact will be less upon those who dispose of specific types of capital property, namely those who fall within the definition of the indexed security investment plan under this Bill, it is only those persons and not the small-scale entrepreneur who are praised in the Speech from the Throne. These are the very people who in large measure have no opportunity to use the advantages of these provisions because their stock is not listed on a recognized stock exchange, the first prerequisite under the Bill.
How are they treated, Mr. Speaker? Well, they are spoken of in other parts of the Throne Speech, perhaps not as directly but certainly by inference. Let us examine the comment which appeared early in the speech where we see:
To compete in the world economy, Canada needs to modernize capital facilities, develop new industries and rebuild plant and equipment.
We are talking about the acquisition or development of capital assets in Canada, which in large measure would, in the normal course of events, be developed or acquired by small business. Yet the last time this House had an opportunity to deal with an amendment to the Income Tax Act-i am talking about Bill C-139 in the first session of this Parliament-the Government was granted the right by regulation amendment to strike out the normal 100 per cent capital cost allowance, depending upon the category of the asset, and only one-half of what normally might be claimed as capital cost allowance was extended to those persons who went out and, in the course of carrying on their business, acquired or developed new capital assets. A detrimental step in the event that the Government ever intended that the small business sector, indeed the entire business sector, go out and acquire and rebuild plant and equipment.
We have an opportunity today to deal with this significant omission. If, indeed, the Government intends to do what it says, recognizing the need to develop new plant and industrial equipment, why are we not told that a taxpayer acquiring those capital assets can in fact claim 100 per cent of the capital cost allowance to which he is entitled, not half of it, in the first year after acquisition? It makes good sense if the Government finally intends to follow through with the promises in the Speech from the Throne to deal with this issue in a proper fashion. However, 1 have grave doubts that the Government intends to do anything other than to continue to demand more of the growth and wealth potential of this country, take it into its own pocket and use it for purposes best known to the Government alone. Of course, in the Speech from the Throne we have an opportunity to hear what some of those purposes are. Government is intent upon continuing to spend on foreign aid some .5 per cent of our GNP by 1985, and .7 per cent by the end of the decade.
We are obliged as Members of this House to examine what the limit of the taxpayers' ability to pay shall be. I drew to the attention of this House the fact that in 1982-we do not have the figures for 1983, but I doubt they are any less-some $42 billion were taken from individuals in this country, and 1 am not talking about corporate taxation, up from $33 billion the year before.
Where is it to end? It will end only when this House has the courage to examine the expenditure plan of government and determine where moneys can best be allocated with a genuine view to reducing tax rates which impose an obligation on the citizens of this nation to turn more and more of their property over to the Government of Canada. I fear that we have become too conditioned to the concept, which I reject, that all property belongs to the state. We are developing in that direction, a concept that the citizen is entitled to use only that which the government permits him to. We know that half of the entire Gross National Product of this country is now spent by government. That leaves the remaining half to be spent by the people who make it, the people who work and generate the wealth, build the homes and factories, turn out the automobiles and furniture and fixtures and make life bearable in Canada.
The Government has intruded in a fashion which we as Members of Parliament have now begun to accept. It was at one time, Mr. Speaker, believed that the intrusion of government into the pockets of the citizen was robbery. The imposition of taxation was an act of thievery. But we no longer regard it that way. We have become so conditioned to expect government to take more and more that there is no voice of alarm raised when the take from individual citizens in this country over a period of one year increases from $33 billion to $42 billion. No one complains. You hear no shouts of alarm. You do not see people at the barricades demanding that government take less and leave them with more.
December 15, 1983

I think it is time this House recognized its responsibilities. Every time the Government spends we should say that part of that money belongs to our constituents. It is my intention to do my utmost to see that we get value for every cent of every dollar which government spends.
We must strike out on a path to accomplish two purposes. We must change the thrust of this Act so that it is understood by the people against whom it is applied, and so that less is taken from the pockets of the citizens of this country. In the Government's mad desire to fill its pockets so that it can spend money in a fashion which it determines, it tramples on the rights of individual citizens in a fashion which I, as a Member of Parliament, find reprehensible.
Before I was elected to Parliament I acted as a tax practitioner. I had an opportunity to see first hand occasions where assessments were issued against a taxpayer one day and the following day a certificate, having the force and effect of a judgment in the Federal Court, was obtained, under the provisions of this Act as they presently stand and are not amended by this Bill. On the day after the issuing of the assessment, a writ of execution is obtained and served and the property of the taxpayer was seized and taken away by the sheriff. Those were business assets, and I suppose that, given the nature of the way in which Members of Parliament might respond to business closure, it would take several of those to make one weep. Then let me tell the House of an elderly woman in Southampton, Ontario who had the misfortune of having a son who made her a gift which permitted her and her husband to acquire a modest home in that town. Part of the proceeds for the purchase of that residence were advanced by herself and her husband. In order to make it easier to raise money by way of mortgage, the son was shown as one of the owners of the residence and he undertook to pay the mortgage. The son did not pay his income tax and left Canada. His parents still reside at that property, but will for only a very brief period of time because the Department of National Revenue has dispatched the sheriff to seize and sell the home out from under a woman in her seventies. The woman herself has never been indebted to the Department of National Revenue.
I told the House, Mr. Speaker, that there is no equity in tax legislation. I can understand the lack of compassion when business assets are seized and sold. But here is a perfect circumstance however where a taxpayer, although she owes no tax on her own account, is going to be put out of her home in the middle of the winter by the assiduous activities of the Department of National Revenue. It is that kind of thing to which this House should direct its attention as it examines remedial steps which should be taken to benefit the people of this country.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am participating in debate rather than posing a
Income Tax Act
question. I should like to speak to this Bill which is now before us since it is an important part of the total economic package as set forth in last April's budget. The tax measures before the House today represent one important element. They are designed to provide the business sector with additional stimulus to assist in the recovery of the Canadian economy. We in Canada, as have so many industrialized countries, have passed through a period of severe economic recession. The response of the Government in the April Budget was to undertake a number of measures funded by the public sector, funded by the Government, and ultimately funded by the taxpayers of Canada, to provide immediate assistance to those most adversely affected by the recession and to finance capital projects which would not only provide employment in the short term, but also assist in providing the infrastructure necessary for further ecomomic recovery. Those measures of which 1 speak of in the public sector have, of course, had the effect of requiring more public financing, and of increasing the level of the federal deficit.
I listened with some interest to the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) when he spoke on this Bill a day or two ago. He drew attention to the current level of the deficit, portraying a gloomy picture of the present deficit financing at the federal level in Canada. He suggested to us that he could see little reason to think that that situation would change in the future. I can understand why he had that thought in mind, because indeed he is committeed to the same policy. He has spoken in terms of support and understanding for the present fiscal policies of the Government. In an intervention in The Globe and Mail a few days ago, he said that if he were in government tomorrow he would follow the same policies now pursued by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). With regard to the deficit itself, he said that the Minister of Finance had little choice but to plan a deficit in the $30 billion range, adding that a big deficit this year is necessary to encourage economic recovery. I am glad, Mr. Speaker, that on the question of the size of the deficit we have that bipartisan understanding and that degree of support for the policies of the Government in providing in the shorter run, employment and economic stimuli through a degree of government spendings.
As Members have noted, and indeed as the previous speaker noted, the real motor for the creation of jobs in our economy is, of course, the private sector. It is the private sector which is provided with stimuli through the tax measures before us today to invest and expand their operations in such a way as to provide both increased employment and to ensure greater productivity in our industry. This is the ultimate answer both to inflation and to our ability to compete in international markets.
We have had some discussion during our review of this Bill about the fact that some time is being taken to bring forward the tax measures arising from the April Budget. There are, of course, several reasons for this. Much of the time of the House has been taken up during the past months by a contentious piece of legislation which involved a prolonged debate. Leaving

December 15, 1983
Income Tax Act
aside the limitations imposed by the timetable in the House itself, we as a government have taken the occasion to give some substance to our commitment to a greater degree of consultation with business and labour about taxation measures.
Members will recall that for a number of years Finance Ministers both from my Party and from the Party of the Official Opposition have committed themselves to improving the ways in which budgets are formulated. They have committed themselves to a process of consultation with regard to tax measures that flow from budgets. That is something new on the Canadian scene. In the specific case of research and development incentives in the April Budget, for example, the government in putting forward, its thinking took the occasion to consult with a wide variety of companies, some very small, some larger, in the research and development area to obtain their views on how best to formulate the exact proposals to promote research and development in Canada.
The area is a difficult one with such a high degree of foreign investment in our country, and there is necessarily a greater degree of research and development centred outside our country since typically large multinational corporations place their research and development either at their corporate headquarters or at the centre of technical excellence in that industry, wherever it may be in the world. One result has been that Canada, with such a high degree of foreign investment, has not been a place in which substantial amounts of research and development have been undertaken. As a result, both the federal Government and in some degree provincial governments, have undertaken to provide greater stimulus to the private sector than one finds in most other industrialized countries. That stimulus embodied in the bill before us was fully explored with those most directly involved in research and development, both in the application and in the innovation area, and the benefits, I think, are reflected in the clauses of the Bill relating to research and development that are now before us.
Equally, at an early stage we as a government put forward the proposals on ISIP which were, in the first instance, developed by a private sector committee. Those proposals from the Lortie Commission were available for discussion by the public for a considerable period, and the benefits of that discussion are again evident in the Bill before us.
In a variety of ways the consultation which the Government has undertaken has enabled the Bill to be improved. We have also had the benefit of the discussions of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs which reviewed some of the measures in this Bill. The conclusions of the committee were of help in assisting the Government in drafting the final wording of the measures now before us.
We have had some discussion today about tax simplification. There has been concern expressed by Members on both sides of the House that our tax system, both personal income tax and corporate income tax, has become increasingly complex. I do not know of anyone who would disagree with that proposition. Who, after all, can be against tax simplification? Obviously everyone is in favour of tax simplification.
The situation we have today, in Canada, and indeed the situation in many industrialized countries, is the result of a cumulative process, of an incremental process whereby at different stages in time it is seemed appropriate to a government in office to bring forth certain tax measures. These act as a stimulus to investment by individuals or by corporations. For example, Governments have brought forward measures intended to recognize the disabled among Canadians, or measures intended to meet the particular needs and problems of one-parent families or the situation of working women. Any number of other measures have been brought forward in tax legislation to take account of the needs of particular people in our society or else to provide stimuli in other areas, and we touched on one a moment ago, that of research and development, which seem to be in the broad public interest.
Not only do those measures themselves introduce complexity into the tax legislation, but additionally each measure carries the need for qualifications or restrictions so as to ensure that the measures are implemented fairly and that no unfair advantage is taken by any taxpayers.
The result of that incremental process of which I spoke is that we have a very complex tax system. The Government has recognized that a stage has been reached when we should look again at simplifying our tax system to ensure that the economic development is not hindered by a complex tax system, particularly in the small business sector, and that the opportunities for the entrepreneurs are enhanced by a simplified tax system.
To that end the Minister of Finance has spoken of his commitment to move in the area of tax simplification. The Government took the initiative to refer that broad question to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic affairs, which I trust will continue to address in the time ahead.
We as a government also sought the advice of a variety of tax practitioners, tax experts, who can contribute to a rational tax simplification. A major conference to that end was sponsored with the Canadian Tax Foundation in Toronto this past summer. Additional work is now proceeding to determine in what ways, particularly in the small business sector, real progress can be made. I say the small business sector because obviously there is a whole range of areas, a spectrum, in which tax simplification is of concern to this Government, but that if one must place priorities on this issue, and it is inevitable that one must, then it seems to us on this side of the House that the area of small business taxation is one that should receive that priority.
I want to say a word about one or two specific areas of the Bill which require special notice. They are intended, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, to help provide stimulus to the private sector, partly in its job-creation activities. I have in mind the investment tax credit. The Bill before the House does not increase the rates of existing tax incentives but it will
December 15, 1983

certainly make the incentives more readily usable by firms undertaking new investments. Presently the investment tax credit provides a reduction in the income tax equal to a percentage of investments in plant and equipment used in manufacturing and resource industries, and I want to include in that farming and fishing. There has been a limit on the use of that tax credit. The Bill now before us removes that limit.
We are also enhancing a taxpayer's ability to carry over unclaimed investment tax credits earned in one year so as to be able to reduce federal tax both in the period ahead and in past years. In effect, we are doing this to provide a greater cash flow to companies, a problem which has been a particular difficulty during the recent period of recession through which Canada has passed. I want to note in passing that we are also extending the investment tax credit to heavy equipment used in the construction industry as one of several stimuli to promote more activity in that vital sector of our economy.
This Bill also provides, as Elon. Members have noted so well, for a new way in which investors contemplating Canadian equity purchases can immunize themselves from the effect of inflation on that part of their earnings represented by capital gains. As I suggested earlier, ISIP was developed in conjunction with the Investment Dealers' Association and with the brokerage industry across Canada. It is a complex program but it is one which the industry is perfectly capable of managing, thanks in part to the technology available today. It can have a very real impact in times of inflation on the investment decisions of Canadians; I say "impact" in a positive sense. The program can offer Canadians a way of sheltering that part of their capital gains on Canadian common shares from the impact of inflation.
Obviously there are a number of other aspects of the Bill with which I could deal today, those parts pertaining to home ownership and the ways in which we hope to provide additional stimulus to farmers and small businessmen through the Small Business Bond which operates through a tax exemption given to lenders. A high proportion of the Small Business Bond program is in fact used by farmers. I suppose, more accurately, that part of the legislation could be called the "agricultural and small business bond".
I have also touched upon the question of stimulus for research and development. I shall not take any more of the time of the House on that point, other than to say that the cumulative effect of all the measures brought forward, which have been the subject of intense discussion across the country in recent months, is to provide additional stimulus to the private sector in its job creation and business expansion efforts.

Mr. Speaker, would the Minister agree that one of the problems in tax simplification is perhaps the tendency to deal with members of the Canadian Tax Foundation? The Minister may not have had an opportunity, as did members of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, to attend the conference in Toronto of which he spoke. It struck me that it was a situation wherein perhaps the
Income Tax Act
Minister was asking the foxes to redesign a henhouse. Has the Minister had an opportunity to read the papers emanating from that Canadian Tax Foundation seminar to determine whether, in his view, he would get very far in tax simplification using these people?

Mr. Speaker, I was in fact at the conference at least part of the time since I was then a member of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
I remember that the Hon. Member opposite and I agreed on that occasion, rather ruefully, that tax simplification seemed to bring in on its train as many complications as the existing legislation itself. I want only to reassure him that those who at the conference often made the subject seem a good deal more complicated than perhaps it needed to be do not represent the only people the Government has been consulting in tax simplification. We have had the benefit of the contributions of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, and of the Canadian Organization for Small Business and the comments of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I do not doubt that the end result will be a simpler process, despite the fact that some members of the tax community have a tendency to see these matters in a complicated way.

That being the case, would the Minister have an opportunity to talk with the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) with respect to a further reference to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs of the tax simplification process, particularly as it relates to small business and indeed medium business?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have already mentioned that to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard).
I hope such a reference can be made. The committee has before it now a number of other references which will necessarily take up some part of its time. I personally would be pleased to have the benefit of the committee's comments on tax simplification.

The Minister spoke about the ISIP matter. Perhaps he was in the House when the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans) indicated that, in his view, the indexation of capital gains should certainly apply to private companies, to private investments and to small investments by people who perhaps create most of the growth and jobs in our country. What effort is the Government taking to bring that type of equity, the equity it seems prepared to give to the clients of investment brokers, to ordinary investment in the country?

The problem as we have found it is that to make effective a system of the type of Hon. Member opposite has in mind-indeed a thought which the Parliamentary Secretary to the House Leader and I share-there has to be some sort of annual evaluation of the asset to enable such a measurement to work. Quite clearly, common stock provides such an opportunity. It is easy to measure the value of the asset if it is expressed in shares of the company. It is a good deal less easy to measure that value in terms of other assets.

December 15, 1983
Income Tax Act
The Hon. Member opposite looks skeptical. The fact is that it is not always possible in any ready way to make that measurement. We are concerned about that problem. The Parliamentary Secretary has already made the comment that we on this side of the House would like to see some of the thinking which has gone into ISIP extended to other forms of assets. However, there is a measurement problem as well as other problems involved in attempting to measure the way in which inflation has affected the values of assets other than commonly-traded shares. I assure the Hon. Member opposite that we are giving consideration to ways in which other assets could be valued so as to attempt to provide the same immunity from inflation which ISIP provides for capital gains on commonly-traded shares.

Mr. Speaker, as far as the valuation is concerned, the Minister will appreciate that the valuation of a farm is the value at which the property sold. That is when the capital gains tax would be payable. The same would apply to a business, factory or store. Why is the Government, prepared as it is to allow those who invest in roughly the 1,100 companies listed on the stock exchange, not prepared to say to those in small business that it will index the gains they realize when they sell in accordance with the CPI and the change in inflation rates over the period of time they held the property? What is so difficult about that?
I point out to the Minister that a 1970 dollar would only have a purchasing power of about 30 cents today. Inflation since 1970 in terms of purchasing power has been about 270 per cent. Most of the gains that are now taxed are really inflation and have nothing to do with gains. That being the case, why will the Government not do the same for small businesses, farmers, fishermen and so on as it is prepared to do for the passive investor who picks up some shares in a listed company?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member opposite is knowledgeable about the general area of taxation, knowledgeable enough to know of the difficulties in establishing bases for valuation of assets other than shares. I have no argument with him in terms of broad equity. I think there is a case to be made for exploring this area, and we are doing that. In what ways can other assets, as I said a moment ago, be effectively valued to provide that same protection? I am afraid that is all I can say at the moment about the subject. We are looking at it and we are trying to develop ways in which we can extend the thinking behind ISIP to other areas.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on Bill C-2, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act and other related Acts. Not only income tax, but the whole tax system is intended to do two things. Even our Conservative friends have at least given lip service to the basic reason for taxation. The first reason is to collect enough revenues to pay for the services that people have come to expect from their governments. This Government has not been doing a particularly good job in the last couple of years when
we have had $30 billion deficits and a collective deficit approaching $200 billion. Therefore, it has not been doing particularly well. Today we are looking at part of the reason for this deficit and also the fairness of the tax system.
The second reason for a taxation system is to redistribute wealth in a fair and equitable manner. Over the years many governments have approached the tax system with these two basics in mind. We should consider these concerns when looking at the amendments before us today.
Changes to the tax system do not always take the form of increases. Most of the changes contained in the Bill will reduce the amount of money that government receives. It favours the corporate structure by a great deal over the personal income tax payer, particularly the lower wage earner. When looking at these changes, there are questions that must be asked. How does this change affect the low-income earner? Who benefits? Is it fair?
The April, 1983 Budget and the subsequent changes in Ways and Means motions can only be described as a financier's budget. This Bill can only be described as a financier's Bill. Let us look at this Bill and the changes being made and try to classify them as to the questions that must be asked, namely how it affects the low-income earner, who will benefit, and is it fair? When we look at this, we see it is very informative.
First, let us look at the phasing down of federal tax reductions. This is a very regressive measure. Granted, there is some reason for it. There is current concern about the process through which people go, but it is regressive. If you pay $200 in income tax, with the federal tax reduction you will end up paying no tax. If you pay $10,000 in income tax, the $200 is a drop in the bucket. Therefore, it does not affect the high-income earner, only the low-income earner. It does not affect those who pay no tax. Therefore, it can only be classed as a very regressive tax. It does not help the low-income earner and benefits the high-income earner. Is that fair? Although this change will increase the amount of money the Government will get, it is not meant to help the low-income earner.
The second point is the elimination of the standard medical and charitable donation deduction. Lower income Canadians cannot afford to make charitable donations totalling $100. They have lost this valuable deduction. We should discuss the fairness of it. If they do not make the donation, should they be allowed the deduction? They were allowed that deduction but now it is being taken away from them. If they cannot afford to make donations, they cannot afford to pay the tax. Consequently, it is a very regressive change. It does not help the low-income earner. If it benefits anybody, it is the high-income earner. Relative to the two, it is not fair.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) asked questions about the indexed security investment plan. That is another concession to higher income Canadians who receive much of their income from investment. Many of us from rural communities are very concerned about the return on investments, as far as farms and so on are concerned, relative to capital gains. There is no consideration in this
December 15, 1983

legislation for any sector but one. Is it fair legislation? Whom does it benefit? It benefits higher income earners and not lower income earners.
I could say almost the very same thing about the special refundable investment tax credit. It does very little for the lower income earners and benefits the higher income earners. It particularly benefits corporations. Many of these corporations are already being financed by the Government through moneys received from increased taxation of middle and lower income Canadians. This particular tax can also be classified as a regressive tax. The share-purchase tax credit is only valuable to those who can afford to buy stocks. A large proportion of the people from whom we collect taxes do not purchase stocks, so it is unfair in that it is aimed only at a small sector of the population.
The Canadian ownership special charge which was brought in under the National Energy Program is also a tax which is unfair. If a person's occupation requires that he use his car, he will pay much more than the fellow who does not need to use his car. A middle or lower income earner will have to spend a larger proportion of his income on that tax because he does not earn as much. So again it is a regressive tax. It affects the lower income earners much more than it affects the high income earners. It helps the corporations and does not help the individual lower income earner. In fact, I think we could look at this whole series of amendments and come to the conclusion that this legislation caters to corporate Canada at the expense of average income earners.
I would like to mention the special recovery tax, a tax which is not contained in this Bill but is contained within a Ways and Means motion of several months ago. That tax increases sales tax by 1 per cent, liquor and tobacco tax by 1 per cent and construction tax by 1 per cent. Again, where does this money really come from? It comes from the consumer rather than from the corporate structure. If I had the time I could go through the entire Bill and show how each of the proposed changes is almost entirely regressive.
We all understand that the word "regressive", when referring to the tax system, means that a tax will benefit the high-income earner and will be detrimental to the low-income earner. In other words, all of these changes have a tendency to make the rich richer and do nothing for the poor or the middle class. This legislation fails to do anything about the redistribution of wealth.
It is obvious from this Bill that the Government has changed its philosophy. The Government has gone from demand side economics to supply side economics. It is taking the Reaganite approach to distribution of wealth. The logic of this theory of economics escapes me. If there are a number of corporations that are overproducing, not producing fully or are unable to sell their full production and are therefore producing at 70 per cent of capacity, should we give them more money or more tax breaks so that they can increase the production of goods which
Income Tax Act
they will be unable to sell? That is the underlying theory of supply side economics.
The Reagan theory of supply side economics is based upon the rather dubious proposition that if we give enough to the rich, some of it will trickle down and perhaps benefit the poor. This has not been seen to happen. In fact, my predecessor as Member of Parliament for Prince Albert used to tell a very pungent story about this. He suggested that another description of the trickle-down theory would be that if one were to feed a horse enough oats, the sparrows would also eat well. That is the supply side theory of economics and it just does not work.
As well, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of other things about this Bill which are illogical, and if I had the time I would like to go into them. However, members of the Official Opposition have dealt very strongly with the complexities of the Bill and I must agree with them. Unfortunately, they are not dealing with those factors in this Bill which perhaps are more important than others.
A great deal of this Bill gives tax breaks to people who are already doing well and we have no guarantee that those tax breaks will increase investment. In fact, we can be fairly sure that they will not increase investment. The massive transfer of revenue to the corporate community has not effectively increased investment in the past. In fact, the chartered accounting firm of Ernst and Whinney, in its submission to the Economic Council of Canada, suggested that most government incentive programs have only a marginal impact on the decision whether or not to invest. Therefore, this can only be recognized as a very marginal subsidy which will affect the economy particularly when most of the plants in the country are operating 30 per cent or 35 per cent below capacity.
There are a number of amendments in this Bill that have not been dealt with which perhaps should have been dealt with. For intance, over the last year or so we have seen a real rash of complaints coming from the farming community. In these days of hardship for the farming community, many farmers who are responsible and good workers have had to take other jobs, or many of them who have had other jobs have attempted to return to farming. In the process, the Department of National Revenue has reclassified those farmers as hobby farmers.
In my constituency, farmers who farm 15 quarters of land are classified as hobby farmers. The economic situation for farmers in the past few years has been so bad that the amount of money they have made from farming those 15 quarters and carrying stock has not been sufficient and the return from their jobs is greater than the return from their farming operations. They may be turning over $100,000 a year on the farming operation and only getting back $15,000 a year and because of that difference are classified as hobby farmers. The other day, I heard from a farmer who has documented that he spends 134 hours on the farm for every 40 hours that he spends working at his job. He works all weekend and works eight or ten hours a day on the farm after his regular working hours. The Bill does not deal with that but it is a major problem. A few years ago it might have been realistic to

December 15, 1983
Income Tax Act
consider five years long enough to develop a farm and to get out of debt, but today a farmer needs 20 or 25 years to get out of debt. In that case, why should he not be able to take an outside job while he gets the farm going?
I am concerned about something else that the Bill does not deal with and I have written to the Minister about it. He has replied that the matter is being considered but so far nothing has been done. Everyone recognizes that the Old Age Security is not enough for senior citizens to live on and many of them derive part of their income from renting their farms or from investments. They are unable to set money aside because they need it all, but in these cases the Department of National Revenue requires them to pay tax on their income, which sometimes is under $15,000, on an incremental basis every three months. If the farm is rented on a share crop basis, which is quite often the case, the senior citizen has no idea whether he will receive any rent at all but, as he paid taxes in past years, he will be required to pay incremental taxes this year. If he has sold the farm, the money may not be forthcoming until the tax year has gone by, but there is nothing in the Act to deal with that situation.
While we are considering the complexity of the Act we should consider establishing some flexibility which would allow a taxpayer to present his case to the Department. In many cases, computers can pick up mistakes. In the case of the child tax credit, if a mistake is made the constituent is never told about it and unless he comes into a Member's office to inquire he will never find out about it.
In light of all these things that are wrong with the Income Tax Act, it is very important that we eliminate the regressive nature of the income tax system and make it less complex so that a taxpayer can know why he is paying tax and for what.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions, comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, like the Hon. Member on this side who spoke earlier, I am not particularly happy to take part in this debate, but changes are required to the Income Tax Act if we are to be fair to the taxpayers of the country, as the Minister said yesterday. I think the word "fairness" should appear in large letters because it is essential that the system be fair to the taxpayer. Too often the taxpayer's rights are forgotten; he is just one individual who sometimes cannot even get a proper hearing when he has a complaint. Today I should like to deal with some real cases, not fictional or hypothetical ones.
Yesterday in the House I put a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) about a particular case. His memory is not too good because, while we have exchanged scores of letters on the subject, he said he could not recall it. I accept that he could not recall it but point out that it has been discussed with him two or three times in the House and also with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray).
This case has been going on since 1975 and once again I will outline the rudiments of it because the situation is so unfair. The individual in question is a new Canadian, a man not versed in the law, who is being penalized to the extent of $1,000. I wonder if members of the Government will be able to see anything fair in this case when I outline it today. According to the Charter of Rights the individual's rights are supposed to be protected. That makes nice reading but I am concerned about what really takes place in the lives of our people. Nobody should be pushed around and made to pay a bill twice, as in this case.
In 1975 this man, a Canadian citizen, through the Mercantile Bank of Canada, mailed a $1,000 cheque to Revenue Canada as an instalment payment on his taxes. The cheque was stamped and cashed by Revenue Canada and the cancelled cheque came back to him. Revenue Canada credited it to his account as an instalment payment. Then, for some reason or other, someone in the Department decided the money was in the wrong account and took it out. When my constituent found out about this he and his accountant went to the Revenue Canada office in Calgary every week, and every week they were told this was just a computer error which would be corrected in no time. Then all the books were moved from Calgary to Winnipeg. They contacted the Winnipeg office and after some time were told that the records had been destroyed and that the case was closed. Is that not a fine way to do business, Mr. Speaker?
Before the files were destroyed, my constituent was in the Mercantile Bank one day and the manager told him that Revenue Canada took $1,000 out of his bank account. He had not been notified; the Department simply went in and confiscated $1,000 from his account. I want to deal with the question of the Department of National Revenue going into private bank accounts later, Mr. Speaker. Because $ 1,000 was owing, it was taken out of his account. He tried to find out where it went. The Department claimed-they did not have any letters-that it had sent it back to the Mercantile Bank in Calgary. I went to the bank but it had no record of the money having been returned.
The bank says that if the Department can show it a letter saying that the $1,000 was sent back to it, it will make it good to the customer. So I went to the Minister, and time and time again 1 have asked him to give me a letter showing that the money was sent back to the Mercantile Bank. Each time he tells me the case is closed, the file is closed. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, the file is not closed. The rights of a Canadian citizen are at stake. That Department went into his bank account and stole that money-if it does not pay it back-and I use that word advisedly. If it does not pay this money back, then it stole that $1,000.
I do not know what happened to that $1,000, whether it was misplaced, sent somewhere without proper identification, or someone stole it, but I know that this $1,000 was paid by this taxpayer and he is entitled to get it back. If we want the
December 15, 1983

Charter of Rights and Freedoms to mean anything to Canadians, Mr. Speaker, let us treat every Canadian as an individual and a decent citizen and let us not try to take money from a hard working citizen, a new Canadian at that. He came to this country expecting something better from his government. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, until that $1,000 is paid back, as long as I have a breath left in my body I am going to fight to get that $ 1,000 returned to him. It is only right and only fair.
Hear, hear!

This action of going into private bank accounts has happened not once but several times. I have here another case where the Department made an error. This citizen had sent two cheques, each in the amount of $1,627.51. He made the payment in January of 1983. In March of 1983 the Department of National Revenue went into his bank account and took out $3,334.51. This was brought to the attention of the Department and I believe it has not been corrected. But I am shocked at the audacity of the Department to go into someone's bank account and take money out when it was its error in the first place. Even if it is not the Department's error, surely when this House of Commons gives the authority to the Department of National Revenue to go into a private bank account and extract money for taxes, it expects the Department to use common horse-sense. Surely the man should be notified and given a warning that this is going to be done. A totalitarian government could not do worse than the actions of this Government against my constituent in Cochrane. He was not even told. To this day he has not been told by the Department. It was mentioned by his bank manager "by the way", as if $1,000 does not mean a lot of hard work to a fellow working in a service station.
I wish this Government would clean up its act in this legislation with respect to going into people's private bank accounts. We send people to jail if they break into a computer. To take money out of someone's bank account is the same thing. The Government has that authority, in my view, only if it has the decency and courtesy to warn the person that it will do that if he will not pay his taxes. He should be told: "We have warned you time and time again and now we are going into your bank account if you do not pay your taxes". That is the decent way to do it. The practice as it is now is heinous and I do not like it at all. This third party demand has its place in some cases but not to the extent it is being used now by the Department of National Revenue; and it certainly should not be done without the knowledge of the person who owns that bank account.
That brings me again to these instalment payments. The previous speaker mentioned this. I believe this Act should state that senior citizens on pensions, in particular, should not be required to make instalment payments. Someone who has plenty of money would come under a different category. Certainly senior citizens should not be required to make instalments before they even receive the money. A senior citizen came to me because he was charged a penalty by the
Income Tax Act
Department of National Revenue for not declaring revenue when he did not even receive that revenue until late in the year. Why should he make instalment payments at the end of March, the end of June and the end of September when the payment came in during November? But he still had to pay a penalty. That case alone shows the unfairness of making senior citizens make instalment payments every three months. Surely it was never intended that senior citizens should have to do that. If they pay the total amount of taxes at the end of the year, that should be good enough for the Department. It is good enough for any grocery store. You pay your bill at the end of the month and it is paid. But it is not good enough for this Government the way it is operating right now.
There is something else about these instalment payments. These penalties are added at the end of the first period, the second period and the third period. I am not talking about senior citizens now; I am talking about ordinary businessmen who have accountants. Many times their income comes in August or September, particularly with farm accounts where farmers do not have money coming in all through the year. They receive it when their wheat goes to the elevator or their cattle goes to market, but they are expected to make instalment payments four times a year, and if they underestimate they are stuck. A penalty is imposed on them. The Department does not make any check on when the revenue came into the farmers' pockets. That is absolutely unfair. I say, Mr. Speaker, after careful thought and deliberation, that if a taxpayer pays his total bill by the end of the year, there should be no penalty, instalment payments or no instalment payments.
The idea of instalment payments was so that the Government could receive the money a little earlier and have the use of the money for nine months, six months or three months ahead of time and it could earn interest during that period. But that is not good enough with this present money-hungry Government. It imposes a penalty at the end of the first period, the end of the second period and so on. Then it totals the whole thing up at the end of the year. If that is fair, then I do not know what fairness is. That is what the Hon. Member for Wellington-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) was talking about yesterday, fairness. If we are going to be fair, let us be fair. But we are not being fair with these instalment payments today.
With respect to capital gains taxes, Mr. Speaker, if I had not been sitting down this morning, I would have fallen down when I heard the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) speaking about capital gains taxes this morning. The man did not know what he was talking about when he said capital gains taxes are of no significance to the businessman or to the farmer. The man is completely wacky in that regard.
I want to give you the facts right now, Mr. Speaker. If that Hon. Member were in the same category, he would expect to have fair treatment. A farmer's nest egg, a farmer's pension, for old age is his farm. He works 10, 20, 30, 40 years, along with his wife and his kids, to build up an asset so that when he is 70 years of age he is going to have a nest egg. He pays taxes on everything he makes as he goes along. Then when he is 70,

December 15, 1983
Income Tax Act
what does the Department do? The farmer sells his farm so he can live the rest of his life at a reasonable standard of living- not in luxury-but half of what he receives has to be shoved into income tax.
Not only that, many farms in western Canada are sold on an instalment basis. A farmer sells to his hired man or his son and he says he will sell his farm and it will be paid for over a period of 10 or 20 years. "Give me enough each year so I can live", he says. But what did the Department say in the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance at the time, I think it was the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen)? They said you pay the total capital gains tax on the selling price, even if the money is not even in your pocket. So hundreds of sales were stalled and elderly people had to stay on the farms because they could not afford to go to the bank and borrow money to pay capital gains taxes.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga North should find out the truth about things before he stands up in the House and says that this is of no value to our people. It is their pension. If we say to Members of this House that their pension is of no value to them, well, you are saying the same thing to a farmer or businessman, that their farm or business is of no value.
Capital gains taxes discourage people, Mr. Speaker. A businessman will say that if he expands his business, when he sells it he is going to get stuck with capital gains taxes. Many people sell before they reach retirement age. They say they do not mind paying a reasonable tax buy they are not going to expand their business and hire another seven people. I cited that example in this House before. A businessman could have hired another seven unemployed people, the business was there, he had the land, he just needed to make the investment. But he said to me: "If you think I am going to work my fingers to the bone and then have the Government take it over, nothing doing. I will work for my wife, my family, my parents, but not to give all this capital gain to the Government". How many other businesses in Canada did not expand? Hundreds, 1 think.
The Government wonders why people are unemployed, yet here its policies are discouraging people from expanding and hiring people. We had better start taking a careful look at some of these things. In any case, capital gains should not be applied to the farm. Farm land is producing food for this nation; it is a valuable asset. In my view, capital gains should be taken off entirely in cases of farm land.
Another point I want to mention before my time is up concerns part-time employment. The Act says that part-time losses from a farming operation are deductible to a maximum of $5,000. I know a businessman in my constituency whose losses on his farm last year were $9,000 but the Government will not give him any credit for that. This Party asked the Government to increase the $5,000; it is years out of date, but nothing happened. If we are going to tax people it should be on their income, and if they had expenses in producing that
income, whether it is part time or full time, they should be able to deduct those expenses.
Another point concerns reassessment. I have a case here where a man's income tax was reassessed the same day by two different people. One officer sent him a letter saying there is no tax required, another officer checked the same file a few hours later and sent him a bill for a few thousand dollars. These reassessments are getting to be ridiculous. Does the Department not know what it is doing?
No.

I think that is right. That is what this taxpayer says. I just wrote a letter to the Minister asking him to check into this case because surely the Minister will not stand for people doing that in any tax office, reassessing and reassessing and reassessing. No taxpayer will know where he stands.
This Act needs a lot of revision, Mr. Speaker. 1 hope many of these points will be brought out in amendments before the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: BLUNDER COMMITTED BY PREMIER OF QUEBEC IN RELATION TO ITALY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps I may also welcome the Chief Electoral Officer, who is from the riding of Lotbiniere.
Madam Speaker, this afternoon I would like to express to the House my sorrow and surprise at the manner in which the Premier of the Province of Quebec is representing the Province abroad.
Today I read in the newspaper La Presse, and that is why I have the paper in front of me, that the President of the Republic of Italy, Mr. Sandro Pertini, was returning his passport to the 1534-1984 celebrations, saying that he was, and I quote:
-very upset about Mr. Levesque's attempts at exploiting his words and the perversely erroneous interpretation he had given.
The article goes on to say:
In protest, Mr. Pertini's advisor gave Mr. Hardy,
-a representative of the Government of Canada, the passport, asking him to return it to Mr. Levesque, who had given it to the President.
Madam Speaker, I am rather surprised that the Premier of a Province like Quebec should think he can afford to say things abroad and then tell us afterwards that it was not as bad as all that, as he said yesterday in the National Assembly.
I think that all these attempts to promote Quebec, including what Mr. Levesque did in Italy, are actually hurting the interests of Quebecers and the Province of Quebec in general. Madam Speaker, I hope that Quebecers will remember this occurrence and remind the Premier of the Province of Quebec of his mistakes.

subtopic: MURDER COMMITTED BY RELEASED SEXUAL OFFENDER
MURDER COMMITTED BY RELEASED SEXUAL OFFENDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last Sunday night on the CTV program, W-5, we saw a prime
example of why Canadians have no trust in the criminal justice system as run by the Government. Canadians witnessed the tragic events surrounding the abduction and murder of 15 year old Corina Carlson of Thunder Bay, by a man who was convicted of sexual offences on five previous occasions and who admitted to seven others. He was turned loose into an unsuspecting community by a justice system which apparently is incapable of protecting, or unwilling to protect innocent members of society.
The murderer's lawyer made a very startling indictment of our system when he alleged that there is no way this could have been prevented. Canadians need to know from the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) whether this allegation is correct and what they intend to do to remedy the situation. Canadians are fed up with the bleeding heart Liberal approach to the administration of justice. They want some action on the protection of society. Mrs. Carlson put it very forcefully and eloquently when she said that the offender has all kinds of rights under this system, but the victims have no rights. I happen to agree with her.

subtopic: ARGENTINA-CALL FOR SUPPORT OF DEMOCRATICALLY ELECTED GOVERNMENT
ARGENTINA-CALL FOR SUPPORT OF DEMOCRATICALLY ELECTED GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, several weeks ago the country of Argentina returned a democratic Government after about ten years of military rule. One of the first things that the new President, Raul Alfonsin, has done, has been to issue a decree saying that the nine generals who were in charge of Argentina during that period will be brought to trial for murder, torture, and other crimes against human rights. Argentina, at this time, is also in a very grave economic situation.
I would like to call upon this House of Commons, and all people interested in justice through law, to support the efforts of the new Government of Argentina. Otherwise the same problem could return. In two countries bordering Argentina- Chile and Uruguay-the same military type of takeover and oppression of people is continuing. It is important that the Government of Argentina know that it has the support of democratic Governments all over the world. I believe that it has taken a great deal of courage to bring to the fore immediately the problems that the generals and the military have caused their own countrymen.

subtopic: AMOUNT OF PUBLIC ASSISTANCE RECEIVED BY RESIDENT IN CONSTITUENCY OF WELLAND
